claim: Fear conditioning is one of the most frequently used laboratory procedures for modeling learning and memory generally, and anxiety disorders in particular.
source: Fear conditioning is one of the most frequently used laboratory procedures for modeling learning and memory generally, and anxiety disorders in particular.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific consensus and the extensive literature on fear conditioning.

claim: The conditional response (CR) used in the majority of fear conditioning studies in rodents is freezing.
source: The conditional response (CR) used in the majority of fear conditioning studies in rodents is freezing.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies in the introduction that have used freezing as the primary measure.

claim: Under certain conditions, running, jumping, or darting replaces freezing as the dominant CR.
source: Recently, it has been reported that under certain conditions, running, jumping, or darting replaces freezing as the dominant CR.
evidence: This claim references recent reports in the literature about alternative defensive behaviors.

claim: Running and darting were primarily a result of nonassociative processes and were actually suppressed by associative learning.
source: Contrary to the prior conclusions, running and darting were primarily a result of nonassociative processes and were actually suppressed by associative learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from multiple experiments with control groups.

claim: Darting and flight were analogous to nonassociative startle or alpha responses that are potentiated by fear.
source: Darting and flight were taken to be analogous to nonassociative startle or alpha responses that are potentiated by fear.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the experimental data and comparison to established concepts in the literature about startle responses.

claim: Associative processes had some impact on the topography of flight behavior.
source: Additionally, associative processes had some impact on the topography of flight behavior.
evidence: This is supported by data showing differences in timing of flight responses between paired and unpaired groups.

claim: Freezing was the purest reflection of associative learning.
source: On the other hand, freezing was the purest reflection of associative learning.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by data showing that freezing was greatest in groups that received CS-US pairings compared to control groups.

claim: When afraid, animals freeze until there is a sudden novel change in stimulation, then burst into vigorous flight attempts.
source: We also uncovered a rule that describes when these movements replace freezing: when afraid, freeze until there is a sudden novel change in stimulation, then burst into vigorous flight attempts.
evidence: This rule is derived from the pattern of behaviors observed across all experiments, particularly the timing of flight responses at stimulus onset.

claim: This rule may also govern the change from fear to panic.
source: This rule may also govern the change from fear to panic.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to broader emotional states.

claim: Freezing reduces the likelihood of detection and attack by a predator.
source: Freezing is a common and adaptive defensive behavior as it reduces the likelihood of detection and attack by a predator (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on the adaptive function of freezing.

claim: Over the last four decades, fear conditioning studies have extensively used freezing more than any other response.
source: Over the last four decades, fear conditioning studies have extensively used one of these defensive behaviors, freezing, more than any other response (Anagnostaras et al., 2010; Bouton and Bolles, 1980; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Grewe et al., 2017; Kim and Fanselow, 1992; Kwon et al., 2015; Nader et al., 2000; Roy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using freezing as the primary measure.

claim: Predatory Imminence Continuum theory states that qualitatively distinct defensive behaviors are matched to the psychological distance from physical contact with a life-threatening situation.
source: An influential model of SSDR selection applied to both humans and rodents is Predatory (or Threat) Imminence Continuum theory, which states that qualitatively distinct defensive behaviors are matched to the psychological distance from physical contact with a life-threatening situation (Bouton et al., 2001; Fanselow and Lester, 1988; Mobbs, 2018; Mobbs et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of an established theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Rodents freeze when they detect a predator but show vigorous bursts of activity to contact by the predator.
source: For example, rodents freeze when they detect a predator but show vigorous bursts of activity to contact by the predator (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on defensive behavior patterns.

claim: Post-encounter defense relates to fear-like states.
source: The former, labeled post-encounter defense, relates to fear-like states.
evidence: This is part of the Predatory Imminence framework supported by citations.

claim: Circa-strike defense relates to panic-like states.
source: The latter, referred to as circa-strike defense, relates to panic-like states (Bouton et al., 2001; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: This is part of the Predatory Imminence framework supported by citations.

claim: In fear conditioning experiments the shock unconditional stimulus (US) models painful contact with the predator and therefore invariably produces circa-strike activity bursts but not freezing.
source: According to this account, in fear conditioning experiments the shock unconditional stimulus (US) models painful contact with the predator and therefore invariably produces circa-strike activity bursts but not freezing (Fanselow, 1982).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from Predatory Imminence theory supported by citation.

claim: Stimuli associated with shock such as an auditory conditional stimulus (CS), model detection of a predator and therefore invariably produce post-encounter freezing as a conditional response (CR) but not activity bursts.
source: On the other hand, stimuli associated with shock such as an auditory conditional stimulus (CS), model detection of a predator and therefore invariably produce post-encounter freezing as a conditional response (CR) but not activity bursts (Fanselow, 1989).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from Predatory Imminence theory supported by citation.

claim: Fadok et al., 2017 used a unique two-component serial CS consisting of a 10 s tone followed immediately by a 10 s white noise ending with a 1 s shock and found that the initial component (tone) produced freezing, while the second component (noise) produced bursts of locomotion and jumping in mice.
source: Fadok et al., 2017 used a unique two-component serial CS consisting of a 10 s tone followed immediately by a 10 s white noise ending with a 1 s shock and found that the initial component (tone) produced freezing, while the second component (noise) produced bursts of locomotion and jumping in mice.
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: Gruene et al., 2015 reported that in rats a tone CS resulted in a burst of locomotion, labeled darting, and this was replicated in subsequent studies.
source: Gruene et al., 2015 reported that in rats a tone CS resulted in a similar burst of locomotion, labeled darting, and this was replicated in subsequent studies (Colom-Lapetina et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes findings from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Fadok et al., 2017 and Gruene et al., 2015 concluded that activity bursts were CRs because they increased over trials during acquisition when CS and US were paired and decreased during extinction when the CS was presented alone.
source: Both previous reports concluded that these activity bursts were CRs because they increased over trials during acquisition when CS and US were paired and decreased during extinction when the CS was presented alone (Fadok et al., 2017; Gruene et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the conclusions from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Increases and decreases in responding during acquisition and extinction could result from nonassociative processes such as sensitization and habituation.
source: While these behavioral patterns are certainly properties of a CR, they are not diagnostic of associative learning as these changes could also result from nonassociative processes such as sensitization and habituation (Rescorla, 1967).
evidence: This is a theoretical point about learning processes supported by citation to Rescorla's work on associative learning.

claim: Hersman et al., 2020 suggested that white-noise-elicited activity burst is mainly a result of the stimulus salience or intensity of the white noise and does not depend on any particular temporal relation to the US.
source: One subsequent study using this serial conditioning procedure in mice has suggested that this white-noise-elicited activity burst is mainly a result of the stimulus salience or intensity of the white noise and does not depend on any particular temporal relation to the US (Hersman et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: Totty et al., 2021 suggested that flight behavior only occurs in contexts in which fear has been established and is a result of associative processes.
source: Another recent study using this procedure in rats has suggested that this flight behavior only occurs in contexts in which fear has been established and is a result of associative processes (Totty et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes findings from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: In Experiment 1, the Replication Group obtained nearly identical results to Fadok et al., 2017.
source: In the nearly exact replication of the conditions used by Fadok et al., 2017, using male and female mice, we obtained nearly identical results with our Replication Group (Table 1, Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the Replication Group, freezing to the initial tone progressively increased over the course of conditioning.
source: In the Replication Group, freezing to the initial tone progressively increased over the course of conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the beginning of training, freezing increased to the white noise but plateaued after a few trials.
source: At the beginning of training, freezing increased to the white noise but plateaued after a few trials.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When freezing plateaued the noise elicited activity bursts, and this pattern maintained throughout acquisition and the beginning of extinction testing.
source: When freezing plateaued the noise elicited activity bursts, and this pattern maintained throughout acquisition and the beginning of extinction testing.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: As extinction testing continued, freezing was maintained while PAR and darting to the noise decreased.
source: As extinction testing continued, freezing was maintained while PAR and darting to the noise decreased.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Activity bursts and darting in no way depended on the use of a serial compound (CS Duration Group).
source: In other words, activity bursts and darting in no way depended on the use of a serial compound.
evidence: This is supported by the data from the CS Duration Group showing similar responses to noise alone.

claim: Even though the noise was never paired with shock it still evoked an activity burst (Stimulus Change Group).
source: What is striking about this finding is that even though the noise was never paired with shock it still evoked an activity burst.
evidence: This is supported by the data from the Stimulus Change Group shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Stimulus Change Group showed greater PAR on trials 2 and 5 compared to the Replication Group.
source: For PAR, a repeated measures ANOVA with Trial, Group, and CS type revealed a main effect of CS type (F[1, 24]=53.121, p<0.001) as well as a Trial X Group interaction (F[15, 360]=1.970, p=0.017) such that Stimulus Change animals showed greater PAR on trials 2 and 5 (p's=0.003, 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For only the Stimulus Change Group, PAR decreased over the session.
source: Further, for only the Stimulus Change Group, PAR decreased over the session (p=0.034).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The Stimulus Change Group darted more than the Replication Group.
source: For darting, a repeated measures ANOVA with Trial, Group, and CS type revealed a main effect of group (F[1, 24]=4.321, p=0.048) such that the Stimulus Change Group darted more than the Replication Group, with no interaction with CS type.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The Stimulus Change Group (no noise-shock pairing) generally shows more flight than the Replication Group (noise-shock pairing).
source: Thus, if there are any differences between Replication and Stimulus Change groups, it is that the Stimulus Change Group (no noise-shock pairing) generally shows more flight than the Replication Group (noise-shock pairing).
evidence: This is based on the statistical comparisons of the experimental data.

claim: These findings strongly implicate nonassociative processes in the activity burst rather than conditioning.
source: These findings strongly implicate nonassociative processes in the activity burst rather than conditioning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that noise-shock pairing was not necessary for activity bursts.

claim: Velocity peaked during the first bins of the noise period and then quickly decreased to more stable levels.
source: Generally, velocity peaked during the first bins of the noise period and then quickly decreased to more stable levels.
evidence: This is supported by the velocity data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Stimulus Change Group trended to have elevated velocity during the first bin of the noise period with trends for higher velocity than the CS Duration Group.
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the Stimulus Change Group trended to have the elevated velocity during the first bin of the noise period with trends for higher velocity than the CS Duration Group (p=0.09) and did have significantly higher velocity than the CS Duration Group during the fifth bin (~2.5 s into the noise; p=0.04).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data.

claim: The strongest noise-elicited flight occurred for the group that received the serial compound stimulus only at test and for which the noise was novel at test.
source: While the noise did not need to be within a serial compound stimulus or even need to be presented during training in order to elicit flight, it is worth noting that the strongest noise-elicited flight occurred for the group that received the serial compound stimulus only at test and for which the noise was novel at test.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the experimental data across groups.

claim: Freezing to the noise was greatest in the mice that received noise-shock pairings (F[3, 28]=11.76, p<0.001).
source: As would be expected for a CR, freezing to the noise was greatest in the mice that received noise-shock pairings (F[3, 28]=11.76, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Significant associative learning was indicated by more noise-elicited freezing in the paired group than the shock-only trained group tested with the noise.
source: Significant associative learning was indicated by more noise-elicited freezing in the paired group than the shock-only trained group tested with the noise.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 4.

claim: The no shock group that was tested with the noise gradually increased freezing over the course of noise testing suggesting that the 75 dB noise itself was aversive to the mice and could support some conditioning of freezing.
source: Interestingly, the no shock group that was tested with the noise gradually increased freezing over the course of noise testing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the 75 dB noise itself was aversive to the mice and could support some conditioning of freezing (i.e. it was a weak US).
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greatest PAR occurred in the pseudoconditioned control (shock only during training) that was tested with the novel noise (F[3, 28]=20.085, p<0.001).
source: The greatest PAR occurred in the pseudoconditioned control (shock only during training) that was tested with the novel noise (F[3, 28]=20.085, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The pseudoconditioned control tested with the novel noise also showed the most darting behavior.
source: The pseudoconditioned control tested with the novel noise also showed the most darting behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 4.

claim: The shock only-noise test group had the highest velocity during the second bin of the noise period (the first second of the CS) with significantly higher velocity than the no shock-noise test, shock only-tone test and noise shock-noise test groups.
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the shock only-noise test group had the highest velocity during the second bin of the noise period (the first second of the CS) with significantly higher velocity than the no shock-noise test (p=0.03), shock only-tone test (p=0.004) and, importantly, the noise shock-noise test groups (p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 2.

claim: Pseudoconditioning is indicated by more activity during the noise test in the previously shocked mice than the no-shock controls tested with the same noise.
source: Pseudoconditioning is indicated by more activity during the noise test in the previously shocked mice than the no-shock controls tested with the same noise.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: While the group that received noise-shock training showed an elevated PAR, the level was significantly less than the pseudoconditioning control (p<0.001).
source: Another striking finding is that while the group that received noise-shock training showed an elevated PAR, the level was significantly less than the pseudoconditioning control (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Not only are activity bursts not conditioned, these data suggest conditioning may actually suppress such activity bursts.
source: Not only are activity bursts not conditioned, these data suggest conditioning may actually suppress such activity bursts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing lower activity bursts in the paired group compared to the pseudoconditioned group.

claim: Flight and darting are primarily a result of nonassociative processes and are likely not CRs.
source: In other words, flight and darting are primarily a result of nonassociative processes and are likely not CRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Across training freezing to the white noise rose, and then plateaued in the paired and unpaired groups, at which point the noise began to elicit activity bursts.
source: As seen in the prior experiments, across training freezing to the white noise rose, and then plateaued in the paired and unpaired groups, at which point the noise began to elicit activity bursts.
evidence: This is supported by the data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the CS only group white noise alone supported low, but consistent levels of freezing but in the shocked groups the noise disrupted freezing to the context.
source: In the CS only group white noise alone supported low, but consistent levels of freezing but in the shocked groups the noise disrupted freezing to the context.
evidence: This is supported by the data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 6.

claim: During training, the paired and unpaired groups showed elevated PAR to the noise (F[3, 28]=29.94, p<0.001 for day 1; F[3, 28]=75.18, p<0.001 for day 2).
source: During training, the paired and unpaired groups showed elevated PAR to the noise (F[3, 28]=29.94, p<0.001 for day 1; F[3, 28]=75.18, p<0.001 for day 2), and increased darting to the noise (F[3, 28]=9.392, p<0.001 for day 1; F[3, 28]=29.746, p<0.001 for day 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: For darting, the paired group showed elevated responding on both day 1 (p=0.017) and on day 2 (p=0.004) compared to the unpaired group.
source: Interestingly, for darting, the paired group showed elevated responding on both day 1 (p=0.017) and on day 2 (p=0.004) compared to the unpaired group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: During testing, activity bursts (measured as both PAR and darting) to the noise were elevated in all groups that received shock (F[3, 28]=13.35, p<0.001 for PAR; F[3, 28] = 8.160, p<0.001 for darting).
source: During testing, activity bursts (measured as both PAR and darting) to the noise were elevated in all groups that received shock (F[3, 28]=13.35, p<0.001 for PAR; F[3, 28] = 8.160, p<0.001 for darting).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The unpaired group had the highest velocity during the first bin of the noise period (the first second) with significantly higher velocity than the CS only group (p=0.007).
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the unpaired group had the highest velocity during the first bin of the noise period (the first second) with significantly higher velocity than the CS only group (p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 3.

claim: In the 16th and 17th bins toward the end of the CS period, the paired group showed the most activity with significantly higher velocity than the CS only group, the shock only group, and the unpaired group.
source: Additionally, in the 16th and 17th bins toward the end of the CS period, the paired group showed the most activity with significantly higher velocity than the CS only group (p=0.002 and p=0.001), the shock only group (p=0.001, p=0.02), and the unpaired group (p<0.001, p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 3.

claim: Pairing noise and shock altered the timing of the activity bursts.
source: That pairing noise and shock altered the timing of the activity bursts is an interesting fact worth considering and suggests that pairing noise and shock may have primarily resulted in a conditional freezing response that in fact competes with/reduces any initial nonassociative activity/bursting to the white noise.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the velocity data showing different timing patterns between paired and unpaired groups.

claim: A large portion of the noise-elicited activity bursts observed is due to nonassociative processes that result in an increase in darting behavior to the noise following shock exposure, regardless of any direct training history of the noise with shock.
source: Taken together, this and the prior experiment using control groups to assess pseudoconditioning reveal that a large portion of the noise-elicited activity bursts observed is due to nonassociative processes that result in an increase in darting behavior to the noise following shock exposure, regardless of any direct training history of the noise with shock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: There does appear to be evidence that pairing noise with shock may further increase or alter the timing of this behavior, but by no means is pairing noise with shock necessary to produce these activity bursts.
source: There does appear to be evidence that pairing noise with shock may further increase or alter the timing of this behavior, but by no means is pairing noise with shock necessary to produce these activity bursts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Within groups that received habituation, a low level of darting to the white noise alone without any shock decreased across day 1 (F[4, 48]=2.887, p=0.026) and increased by the end of the second day of habituation (F[4, 48]=2.793, p=0.36).
source: During the 2 days of habituation, interestingly, we found that within groups that received habituation, a low level of darting to the white noise alone without any shock decreased across day 1 (F[4, 48]=2.887, p=0.026) and increased by the end of the second day of habituation (F[4, 48]=2.793, p=0.36; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Freezing to the white noise increased over habituation trials, again showing that this white noise stimulus alone can act as a US.
source: Concurrently, freezing to the white noise increased over habituation trials, again showing that this white noise stimulus alone can act as a US.
evidence: This is supported by the data from Experiment 4.

claim: Darting occurred to the white noise at the start of habituation when the CS was very novel, and at the end of habituation once the white noise alone was able to support some level of fear.
source: It is interesting that darting occurred to the white noise at the start of habituation when the CS was very novel, and at the end of habituation once the white noise alone was able to support some level of fear.
evidence: This is an observation from the data in Experiment 4.

claim: Comparing the two shock only groups during test, the noise disrupted freezing more than tone.
source: Comparing the two shock only groups during test, the noise disrupted freezing more than tone.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Within paired groups (H-paired and C-paired), prior habituation to the white noise increased freezing (F[1, 24]=5.701, p=0.025) and decreased noise-elicited darting (F[1, 24]=5.130, p=0.033) throughout acquisition.
source: Within paired groups (H-paired and C-paired), we found that throughout acquisition and particularly on the second day of training (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), prior habituation to the white noise increased freezing (F[1, 24]=5.701, p=0.025) and decreased noise-elicited darting (F[1, 24]=5.130, p=0.033), as predicted if prior exposure to the CS functions to reduce any partially novelty-driven darting.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: At test, for freezing, there was a main effect of pairing (F[1, 24]=11.306, p=0.003), such that animals who received white noise paired with shock froze more than animals who only received shock during acquisition.
source: At test (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), for freezing, we found a main effect of pairing (F[1, 24]=11.306, p=0.003), such that animals who received white noise paired with shock froze more than animals who only received shock during acquisition, again indicative that noise-elicited freezing is a conditional behavior that results from associative learning.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: For darting behavior, there was a habituation X pairing interaction (F[1, 28]=4.939, p=0.035) such that pairing white noise with shock increased darting within habituated animals (p=0.033), and that habituation reduced darting within animals who only received shock during training (p=0.045).
source: For darting behavior, we found a habituation X pairing interaction (F[1, 28]=4.939, p=0.035) such that pairing white noise with shock increased darting within habituated animals (p=0.033), and that habituation reduced darting within animals who only received shock during training (p=0.045).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The white noise acts as a US on its own and needs not be paired with shock to produce darting at test.
source: These results reveal multiple points of interest. First, and as shown in prior experiments, the white noise acts as a US on its own and needs not be paired with shock to produce darting at test.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Prior experience with the white noise, through habituation, actually reduced this darting at test.
source: Furthermore, prior experience with the white noise, through habituation, actually reduced this darting at test.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Pairing white noise with shock can further increase darting behavior at test, at least within animals who have already experienced the noise during habituation.
source: Additionally, in this experiment, we do again show evidence that pairing white noise with shock can further increase darting behavior at test, at least within animals who have already experienced the noise during habituation.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The timing of the darting response in paired groups is fundamentally altered compared to shock only groups.
source: Again, as with Experiment 3 (Figure 7), the timing of the darting response in paired groups is fundamentally altered compared to shock only groups (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the velocity data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The magnitude/frequency of the initial activity burst to the noise appears to be reduced in the paired groups, and increased levels of activity bursts during the latter portion of the CS account for any differences/increases in overall numbers of darts.
source: The magnitude/frequency of the initial activity burst to the noise appears to be reduced in the paired groups, and increased levels of activity bursts during the latter portion of the CS account for any differences/increases in overall numbers of darts.
evidence: This is based on the velocity data from Experiment 4.

claim: The shock only groups had significantly higher velocity during the first three bins of the noise than the paired groups (p's=0.02, 0.03, 0.005, respectively).
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the shock only groups had significantly higher velocity during the first three bins of the noise than the paired groups (p's=0.02, 0.03, 0.005, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 4.

claim: Within the nonhabituated groups, pairing noise and shock significantly reduced the velocity throughout test trials (p<0.001).
source: Post hoc analysis on the pairing X habituation interaction reveals that within the nonhabituated groups, pairing noise and shock significantly reduced the velocity throughout test trials (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 4.

claim: Within shock only groups, habituation reduced the velocity throughout test trials (p<.001).
source: Additionally, within shock only groups, habituation reduced the velocity throughout test trials (p<.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the velocity data from Experiment 4.

claim: Exposure to the noise CS (through pre-exposure and/or through pairing CS and US) reduces noise-elicited activity bursts and flight/darting behavior, that is, darting is enhanced by novelty.
source: These results are exactly what would be predicted if exposure to the noise CS (through pre-exposure and/or through pairing CS and US) in fact reduces noise-elicited activity bursts and flight/darting behavior, that is, darting is enhanced by novelty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The magnitude of response to shock was greater than to tone (p<0.0001) and to noise (p<0.0001), and darts to the noise tended to be stronger than darts to the tone (p=0.043).
source: Generally, there was an effect of stimulus on response magnitude (W[2, 123.2]=105.3, p<0.0001). The magnitude of response to shock was greater than to tone (p<0.0001) and to noise (p<0.0001), and darts to the noise tended to be stronger than darts to the tone (p=0.043).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the dart magnitude data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Within a given single CS presentation, the magnitude of the response for the first dart was greater than for the second dart (t=2.641, df = 64, p=0.01).
source: On average, within a given single CS presentation, the magnitude of the response for the first dart was greater than for the second dart (t=2.641, df = 64, p=0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the dart magnitude data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Darts that occurred early during the initial CS onset were larger in magnitude than those that occurred later in the session, suggesting that these two responses may in fact be distinct types of flight behavior.
source: An omnibus ANOVA with group and stimulus period (early vs late) revealed a significant effect of stimulus period (F[1, 331]=16.23, p<0.0001) with no effects of/interaction with group. Darts that occurred early during the initial CS onset were larger in magnitude than those that occurred later in the session, suggesting that these two responses may in fact be distinct types of flight behavior (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the dart timing data shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: The rule is: when in a state of fear (post-encounter defense) sudden stimulus change provokes panic-like circa-strike defenses proportional to stimulus intensity and novelty.
source: The rule is: when in a state of fear (post-encounter defense) sudden stimulus change provokes panic-like circa-strike defenses proportional to stimulus intensity and novelty.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental data across all experiments.

claim: Like shock, both tone and noise disrupted ongoing freezing, the noise did so for longer than the tone, and noise on its own was able to support a minimal level of fear conditioning.
source: Like shock, both tone and noise disrupted ongoing freezing, the noise did so for longer than the tone (Figure 10), and noise on its own was able to support a minimal level of fear conditioning (Figure 6, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Novelty of the stimuli is an important factor and familiarity with the CS during conditioning and/or habituation reduced CS novelty for the test.
source: Novelty of the stimuli is an important factor and familiarity with the CS during conditioning and/or habituation reduced CS novelty for the test.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, particularly from Experiment 4.

claim: The mice that received noise-shock pairings and were tested with noise showed lower flight to the noise than mice trained only with shock and then received noise for the first time.
source: In the experiments presented here, the mice that received noise-shock pairings and were tested with noise showed lower flight to the noise than mice trained only with shock and then received noise for the first time.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiments 2-4.

claim: Prior habituation to the noise or experience with the noise during training (i.e. paired and unpaired groups) further reduced noise-elicited flight at test.
source: Additionally, prior habituation to the noise or experience with the noise during training (i.e. paired and unpaired groups) further reduced noise-elicited flight at test.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: Hull, 1934 cautioned conditioning researchers that it is important to distinguish true conditional responses from unconditional responses to the CS, which he named alpha responses.
source: Hull, 1934 cautioned conditioning researchers that it is important to distinguish true conditional responses from unconditional responses to the CS, which he named alpha responses.
evidence: This is a reference to a historical concept in conditioning research.

claim: Alpha responses occur at the onset of the CS, rather than the time of the expected US.
source: These alpha responses occur at the onset of the CS, rather than the time of the expected US.
evidence: This is a description of the alpha response concept.

claim: In eyeblink studies alpha responses are excluded from analysis by omitting any responses that occur at the beginning of the CS.
source: Typically, in eyeblink studies alpha responses are excluded from analysis by omitting any responses that occur at the beginning of the CS.
evidence: This is a description of standard practice in eyeblink conditioning studies.

claim: Our darting responses almost exclusively occurred at CS onset and there were rarely any US anticipatory-like responses.
source: Our darting responses almost exclusively occurred at CS onset and there were rarely any US anticipatory-like responses.
evidence: This is based on the timing data from all experiments.

claim: Traditional Pavlovian analyses for ballistic CRs would have categorized darting as an unconditional alpha response and not a bona fide CR.
source: Thus, traditional Pavlovian analyses for ballistic CRs would have categorized darting as an unconditional alpha response and not a bona fide CR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of darting responses and comparison to established criteria for CRs.

claim: Our interpretation that noise unconditionally elicits a ballistic activity burst bears some relationship to the unconditional acoustic startle response.
source: Our interpretation that noise unconditionally elicits a ballistic activity burst bears some relationship to the unconditional acoustic startle response.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: Loud noises will elicit an unconditional startle response that wanes with repeated presentations of that noise (i.e. habituation).
source: Loud noises will elicit an unconditional startle response that wanes with repeated presentations of that noise (i.e. habituation; e.g. Davis, 1980; Hoffman and Fleshler, 1963; Leaton, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on acoustic startle.

claim: The unconditional startle response to the loud noise can be potentiated if the loud noise is delivered in the presence of a cue or a context that has been associated with shock/fear.
source: The unconditional startle response to the loud noise can be potentiated if the loud noise is delivered in the presence of a cue or a context that has been associated with shock/fear (Brown et al., 1951; Davis, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on fear-potentiated startle.

claim: We observed an unconditional noise-elicited response that also decreased with habituation (Experiment 4).
source: While our 75 dB noise stimulus is less intense than the 98–120 dB noise used in typical acoustic startle studies, we observed an unconditional noise-elicited response that also decreased with habituation (Experiment 4).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Our data and those of Totty et al., 2021 indicate that these responses require a fearful context in order to occur.
source: Furthermore, our data and those of Totty et al., 2021 indicate that these responses require a fearful context in order to occur.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and comparison to findings from Totty et al., 2021.

claim: Perhaps the low intensity noise is below threshold to elicit a startle response on its own, but a fearful context potentiates this unconditional startle response and brings it above threshold.
source: Perhaps the low intensity noise is below threshold to elicit a startle response on its own, but a fearful context potentiates this unconditional startle response and brings it above threshold.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Totty et al., 2021 found that inactivation of the central nucleus or the bed nuclei of the stria terminalis disrupts the flight response.
source: Totty et al., 2021 found that inactivation of the central nucleus or the bed nuclei of the stria terminalis disrupts the flight response.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: The central nucleus and the bed nuclei of the stria terminalis have been shown to be important mediators of fear's ability to potentiate startle.
source: These two regions have been shown to be important mediators of fear's ability to potentiate startle (e.g. Campeau and Davis, 1995; Davis and Walker, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on the neural basis of fear-potentiated startle.

claim: Fadok et al., 2017 reported that it is corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) expressing cells, but not somatostatin expressing cells, within the central nucleus that support flight behavior.
source: Furthermore, Fadok et al., 2017 reported that it is corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) expressing cells, but not somatostatin expressing cells, within the central nucleus that support flight behavior.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: There is extensive data implicating CRH and fear potentiated startle.
source: Again, there is extensive data implicating CRH and fear potentiated startle (Lee and Davis, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neither Fadok et al., 2017 nor Gruene et al., 2015 included any controls for nonassociative behavior, which is something required in order to conclude that a response is conditional.
source: Neither Fadok et al., 2017 nor Gruene et al., 2015 included any controls for nonassociative behavior, which is something required in order to conclude that a response is conditional (Rescorla, 1967).
evidence: This is a critique of prior studies based on established principles of conditioning research.

claim: Increases in responding with successive shocks could arise via sensitization and decreases in responding when shocks are omitted could arise from habituation.
source: For example, increases in responding with successive shocks could arise via sensitization and decreases in responding when shocks are omitted could arise from habituation.
evidence: This is based on established principles of nonassociative learning.

claim: Shocks, by conditioning fear to the context, sensitize or potentiate the darting response and repeated presentations of the noise alone cause the response to habituate.
source: Shocks, by conditioning fear to the context, sensitize or potentiate the darting response and repeated presentations of the noise alone cause the response to habituate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the experimental data.

claim: Just giving shocks conditioned fear to the context such that when the noise was presented for the first time during test it caused a strong activity burst.
source: Just giving shocks conditioned fear to the context such that when the noise was presented for the first time during test it caused a strong activity burst.
evidence: This is supported by the data from the pseudoconditioning control groups.

claim: The behavior gradually decreased during testing because repeated presentations of the noise led to habituation of this unconditional response.
source: The behavior gradually decreased during testing because repeated presentations of the noise led to habituation of this unconditional response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of responding during testing.

claim: Pairing a stimulus (noise in this case) with another stimulus (shock in this case) is known to reduce the magnitude of habituation.
source: However, it would be expected that habituation would be greater in the unpaired group because pairing a stimulus (noise in this case) with another stimulus (shock in this case) is known to reduce the magnitude of habituation (Pfautz et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on habituation.

claim: This reduction in habituation is observed even if the second stimulus is not an unconditional stimulus.
source: This reduction in habituation is observed even if the second stimulus is not an unconditional stimulus (Pfautz et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on habituation.

claim: Pairing a habituated stimulus with a US can also cause a return of the habituated alpha response, and this loss of habituation is not observed when the two stimuli are not paired.
source: Additionally, pairing a habituated stimulus with a US can also cause a return of the habituated alpha response, and this loss of habituation is not observed when the two stimuli are not paired (Holland, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on habituation and conditioning.

claim: The difference between the paired and unpaired groups reported by Totty et al., 2021 is likely due to differential habituation of the noise during training.
source: Thus, the difference between the paired and unpaired groups reported by Totty et al., 2021 is likely due to differential habituation of the noise during training.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from Totty et al., 2021 based on habituation principles.

claim: Totty et al.'s additional habituation to the SCS in an alternate context prior to SCS or US-only training is a potential explanation for the difference between their findings and the current study.
source: It is possible that Totty et al.'s additional habituation to the SCS in an alternate context prior to SCS or US-only training is a potential explanation for this difference.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: The use of a serial tone-noise compound may have served to further reduce a startle response to the noise in Totty et al. through pre-pulse startle inhibition.
source: The use of a serial tone-noise compound may have also served to further reduce a startle response to the noise in Totty et al. It is well known that if a startle stimulus is preceded by another stimulus, the startle response is reduced in a phenomenon called pre-pulse startle inhibition (Louthan et al., 2020; Groves et al., 1974).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on established principles of startle inhibition.

claim: Two factors may contribute to Totty et al.'s failure to see darting behavior in the animals that did not receive SCS-shock pairings: the use of habituation prior to conditioning and the use of a two-stimulus compound.
source: Thus, two factors may contribute to Totty et al.'s failure to see darting behavior in the animals that did not receive SCS-shock pairings: the use of habituation prior to conditioning and the use of a two-stimulus compound.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: Another factor that may be important is species, with the amount of darting seen in studies using mice being greater than in studies using rats.
source: Another factor that may be important is species. Overall, the amount of darting seen in the studies using mice (Fadok et al., 2017; Hersman et al., 2020; the present study) was greater than in the studies using rats (Gruene et al., 2015; Totty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison of findings across studies using different species.

claim: Cue-elicited locomotion behaviors in rats in previous studies may preferentially be 'movement' that is part of the freezing suite of behaviors, which include locomotion to an ideal thigmotaxic place to freeze.
source: Beyond this potential explanation, as mentioned above and detailed below, there are likely at least two different topographical types of locomotion occurring, and such cue-elicited locomotion behaviors in rats in previous studies may preferentially be 'movement' that is part of the freezing suite of behaviors, which include locomotion to an ideal thigmotaxic place to freeze (e.g. Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the concept of freezing as an integrated behavior.

claim: Associative processes would be expected to alter/increase locomotion that supports/is a part of freezing behavior.
source: Associative processes would be expected to alter/increase such increased locomotion as it supports/is a part of freezing behavior.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the concept of freezing as an integrated behavior.

claim: Freezing is not simply immobility but is an integrated behavior where rats first move to the closest, easily accessible, location appropriate for freezing.
source: Elsewhere we pointed out that the dominant post-encounter behavior, freezing, is not simply immobility (Fanselow and Lester, 1988). Rather, it is an integrated behavior where rats first move to the closest, easily accessible, location appropriate for freezing (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on the nature of freezing behavior.

claim: Rats typically freeze against a wall, especially a corner with its two walls.
source: Typically, this location is against a wall, especially a corner with its two walls (de Oca et al., 2007; Grossen and Kelley, 1972; Sigmundi, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on freezing location preferences.

claim: Freezing and thigmotaxis constitute an integrated behavioral module.
source: In other words, freezing and thigmotaxis constitute an integrated behavioral module (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on freezing behavior.

claim: When an especially appropriate freezing location, a dark cave, was available rats moved to the cave and froze more than when it was not.
source: Indeed, when an especially appropriate freezing location, a dark cave, was available rats moved to the cave and froze more than when it was not (de Oca et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on freezing location preferences.

claim: It would be most inappropriate to characterize the movements needed for thigmotaxis as competing with freezing as they are an integral part of freezing.
source: Therefore, it would be most inappropriate to characterize the movements needed for thigmotaxis as competing with freezing. They are an integral part of freezing.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the concept of freezing as an integrated behavior.

claim: The slower second movement after stimulus onset was directed at a corner and once there the animal became immobile.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the slower second movement after stimulus onset was directed at a corner and once there the animal became immobile.
evidence: This is based on observation of the behavior in the experiments.

claim: Since these movements are part of the freezing module and shock-associated conditional stimuli are one of the most effective ways to drive the freezing module, it is not surprising that they may be more frequent in animals that had sound-shock pairings.
source: Since these movements are part of the freezing module and shock-associated conditional stimuli are one of the most effective ways to drive the freezing module, it is not surprising that they may be more frequent in animals that had sound-shock pairings (Figures 4—8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the concept of freezing as an integrated behavior and the experimental data.

claim: The movements seen by Totty et al., 2021 exclusively in animals that were conditioned were largely this type of movement (thigmotaxis-related).
source: We conjecture that the movements seen by Totty et al., 2021 exclusively in animals that were conditioned were largely this type of movement.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of findings from Totty et al., 2021.

claim: It is likely that the flight behavior in rats observed by other groups is thigmotaxis-related movement as Mitchell et al. report that the majority of their CS-elicited darting occurs late in the CS presentation, about 7–10 s into a 30 s tone CS.
source: Further, it is likely that the flight behavior in rats observed by other groups (Colom-Lapetina et al., 2019; Gruene et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 2021) is this type of movement as Mitchell et al. report that the majority of their CS-elicited darting occurs late in the CS presentation, about 7–10 s into a 30 s tone CS.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing of darting in prior studies.

claim: Circa-strike behavior occurs at or immediately before contact with the predator and represents a vigorous evasive movement away from the predator.
source: Circa-strike behavior occurs at or immediately before contact with the predator and represents a vigorous evasive movement away from the predator.
evidence: This is a description of circa-strike behavior based on the Predatory Imminence framework.

claim: The most effective circa-strike eliciting stimulus in the laboratory setting is shock, as it is directly analogous to painful contact.
source: The most effective circa-strike eliciting stimulus in the laboratory setting is shock, as it is directly analogous to painful contact.
evidence: This is based on the Predatory Imminence framework and experimental observations.

claim: The movement to shock onset is on average the highest velocity movement we observed.
source: As can be seen in Figure 9A–B, the movement to shock onset is on average the highest velocity movement we observed.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The activity burst to shock is highly protean and poorly directed, sometimes looking as if the animal is bouncing off the walls.
source: The activity burst to shock is highly protean and poorly directed, sometimes looking as if the animal is bouncing off the walls (Fanselow, 1982).
evidence: This is based on observation of the behavior and citation to prior work.

claim: When the animal is in the post-encounter fear mode (freezing), the threshold for activity bursts shifts such that sudden stimuli that would not normally cause an activity burst now do so.
source: We argue here that when the animal is in the post-encounter fear mode (freezing), the threshold for these bursts of activity shifts such that sudden stimuli that would not normally cause an activity burst now do so.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: These high velocity movements to tone and noise at stimulus onset are nonassociative responses as they were greatest in animals that never had the sound paired with shock and decreased with familiarity to the stimulus.
source: These are the high velocity movements we see to the noise and the tone at stimulus onset (Figure 9). These are nonassociative responses as they were greatest in animals that never had the sound paired with shock and decreased with familiarity to the stimulus (Figures 5, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: The difference between the stimuli (tone, noise, shock) in eliciting activity bursts seems quantitative, such that shock > noise > tone.
source: The difference between the stimuli seems quantitative, such that shock > noise > tone, but note that in the violin plot some noise-elicited bursts are as fast as the fastest shock responses and many of the shock-elicited bursts overlapped in velocity with those triggered by tone.
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 9.

claim: In all cases, these movements (circa-strike activity bursts) seemed protean and undirected.
source: In all cases, these movements seemed protean and undirected.
evidence: This is based on observation of the behavior.

claim: When an animal is afraid, any sudden change in stimulation can cause them to shift from post-encounter responses, like freezing, toward more circa-strike responses, like undirected flight.
source: Rather than thinking about whether a cue needs to procedurally be a CS or a US to support darting, the data support the hypothesis that when an animal is afraid, any sudden change in stimulation can cause them to shift from post-encounter responses, like freezing, toward more circa-strike responses, like undirected flight.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: It is a sudden change in stimulation, regardless of the conditional/unconditional properties of the cue, that elicits flight behavior.
source: Thus, it is a sudden change in stimulation, regardless of the conditional/unconditional properties of the cue, that elicits flight behavior.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Initial reports suggest a sex difference in noise-elicited flight behavior such that female rats show more of this behavior than males.
source: Initial reports suggest a sex difference in this noise-elicited flight behavior such that female rats show more of this behavior than males (Gruene et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of findings from prior studies.

claim: Within each experiment, we found no sex differences between male and female mice for the PAR and darting measures of flight behavior.
source: Within each experiment, we found no such sex differences between male and female mice for the PAR and darting measures of flight behavior, and Totty et al., 2021 similarly found no sex differences in such behavior in male and female rats.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from all experiments.

claim: Totty et al., 2021 found no sex differences in flight behavior in male and female rats.
source: Within each experiment, we found no such sex differences between male and female mice for the PAR and darting measures of flight behavior, and Totty et al., 2021 similarly found no sex differences in such behavior in male and female rats.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a prior study.

claim: In pooled analysis across all groups that received noise-shock pairings, there were no sex differences in flight to the white noise across the 2 days of acquisition for PAR.
source: In this analysis, again, we saw no sex differences in flight to the white noise across the 2 days of acquisition for PAR (day 1: F[1, 29]=0.323, p=0.58; day 2: F[1, 29]=0.507, p=0.48).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pooled data from all experiments.

claim: For darting, there were no impacts of sex on day 1 of acquisition in pooled analysis.
source: For darting, there were no impacts of sex on day 1 (F[1, 29]=0.009, p=0.92).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pooled data from all experiments.

claim: On day 2 of acquisition, there was a trend for a main effect of sex and CS presentation X sex interaction, such that males darted more than females on the second CS presentation.
source: On day 2, there was a trend for a main effect of sex (F[1, 29]=3.752, p=0.06) and CS presentation X sex interaction (F[4, 116]=2.558, p=0.042), such that males darted more than females on the second CS presentation.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pooled data from all experiments.

claim: There were no sex differences across testing to the white noise in extinction for both PAR and darting in pooled analysis.
source: We further observed no sex differences across testing to the white noise in extinction for both PAR (F[1, 20]=0.099, p=0.76) and darting (F[1, 13]=1.397, p=0.258).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pooled data from all experiments.

claim: We show no major sex differences other than a potential increase in male darting on day 2 of acquisition.
source: Thus, we show no major sex differences other than a potential increase in male darting on day 2 of acquisition.
evidence: This is a summary of the sex difference analyses.

claim: Perhaps initial reports of sex differences with more frequent darting in females could be explained by differences in handling and stress provided to females as a result of monitoring estrous phase.
source: Perhaps initial reports of sex differences with more frequent darting in females could be explained by differences in handling and stress provided to females as a result of monitoring estrous phase, a potentially stressful procedure for the animals for which there is not an ideal control in males.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: Gruene et al., 2015, Colom-Lapetina et al., 2019, and Mitchell et al., 2021, generally find very low levels of darting, with a majority of animals classified as nondarters.
source: It is worth noting that Gruene et al., 2015, Colom-Lapetina et al., 2019, and Mitchell et al., 2021, generally find very low levels of darting, with a majority of animals classified as nondarters.
evidence: This is a description of findings from prior studies.

claim: With the procedure used here, and in mice, we generally do not observe different subpopulations of darters vs nondarters.
source: With the procedure used here, and in mice, we generally do not observe different subpopulations of darters vs nondarters (Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 11.

claim: All animals across all experiments were shown to dart at least once and would be classified as darters using the criteria set forth in Gruene et al., 2015.
source: While there is certainly variation in the level of darting between animals, all animals across all experiments were shown to dart at least once and would be classified as darters using the criteria set forth in Gruene et al., 2015.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from all experiments.

claim: We show some evidence that darts to the tone may be less strong than darts to the noise.
source: Finally, while we show no major differences in tone-elicited flight vs noise-elicited flight, we do show some evidence that darts to the tone may be less strong than darts to the noise (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Perhaps there are species differences in stimulus-evoked flight behavior, such that tone-elicited flight in rats is more sensitive to impacts of sex.
source: Perhaps there are species differences in such stimulus-evoked flight behavior, such that tone-elicited flight in rats is more sensitive to impacts of sex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: Some have characterized freezing as a passive response that occurs because no other response is available.
source: Some have characterized freezing as a passive response (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1969; Fadok et al., 2017; Gozzi et al., 2010; Gruene et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2016) that occurs because no other response is available (Blanchard, 1997; Blanchard et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a description of a view in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Because motion is often the releasing stimulus for predatory attacks it is the best thing for a small mammal like a rat or a mouse to do when a predator is detected and will only be replaced if there is a change consistent with contact.
source: However, because motion is often the releasing stimulus for predatory attacks it is the best thing for a small mammal like a rat or a mouse to do when a predator is detected and will only be replaced if there is a change consistent with contact (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on the adaptive function of freezing.

claim: Rodents choose locations in which to freeze such as corners or objects (thigmotaxis).
source: Rodents choose locations in which to freeze such as corners or objects (thigmotaxis) (Grossen and Kelley, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on freezing behavior.

claim: The current data show that the freezing rodent also prepares to react to sudden stimulus change.
source: The current data show that the freezing rodent also prepares to react to sudden stimulus change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There is nothing passive about freezing.
source: There is nothing passive about freezing.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion based on the findings and the concept of freezing as an integrated behavior.

claim: Subjects for all experiments included 120 C57BL/6NHsd mice, aged 9–11 weeks of age and purchased from Envigo.
source: Subjects for all experiments included 120 C57BL/6NHsd mice (Experiment 1, n=24; Experiment 2, n=32; Experiment 3, n=32; Experiment 4, n=32), aged 9–11 weeks of age and purchased from Envigo.
evidence: This is a description of the subjects used in the study.

claim: This C57BL/6NHsd strain was chosen to match that of Fadok et al., 2017.
source: This C57BL/6NHsd strain was chosen to match that of Fadok et al., 2017.
evidence: This is a methodological decision to enable comparison with prior work.

claim: Each group consisted of four male and four female mice.
source: Each group consisted of four male and four female mice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A necessary/powered group sample size of 8 was calculated based on both years of data in our lab that suggests n=8 is sufficient to detect such behavioral differences in fear conditioning studies and on the recent articles in the literature using this procedure.
source: A necessary/powered group sample size of 8 was calculated based on both years of data in our lab that suggests n=8 is sufficient to detect such behavioral differences in fear conditioning studies and on the recent articles in the literature using this procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the power analysis for the study.

claim: No effects of sex were observed in initial comparisons/ANOVAs.
source: For this and all experiments described below, no effects of sex were observed in initial comparisons/ANOVAs (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analyses.

claim: Sex was removed as a factor in subsequent statistical analyses.
source: Sex was thus removed as a factor in subsequent statistical analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical approach.
